explain.say: Venom is made in glands behind a snake's eyes that evolved from saliva glands. When it bites, muscles squeeze the gland and venom flows through grooved or hollow fangs, like a syringe.

faq.a: Venom is made in a pair of glands at the back of the upper jaw, behind the eyes. They evolved from saliva glands, and muscles around them squeeze venom through the fangs when the snake bites.
asks: Are venom glands like saliva glands?

faq.q: What is snake venom made of?
faq.a: Venom is a mixture of dozens of proteins and enzymes, each targeting a different part of the body, such as nerves, muscles or blood. Different species have very different mixtures.
asks: Why is snake venom a cocktail?

faq.a: Neurotoxins block the messages passing from nerves to muscles. The muscles stop working, causing paralysis, and if the breathing muscles stop, the animal cannot breathe.
Haemotoxins attack the blood and tissues. Some stop blood clotting so wounds keep bleeding, others make blood clot wrongly, and some break down blood vessels and muscle around the bite.
asks: Why do some snake bites bleed a lot?

faq.a: Tiny, safe doses of venom are injected into an animal such as a horse or sheep. Its body makes antibodies, which are collected from its blood and purified. Given to a bitten person, they neutralise the venom.
asks: How do you treat a snake bite?

facts: Snake venom glands are modified salivary glands, and venom is a mixture of many proteins.
The World Health Organization estimates that snakebites kill roughly 81,000 to 138,000 people each year.
